summary: CAIRN (Nankai, Tencent Security Yunding Lab, Tsinghua) coordinates agents through a shared, persistent fact-intent DAG: a reasoner reads verified facts and proposes intents (exploration branches citing their supporting facts), and up to six asynchronous workers execute intents and submit new facts. It is compared with 'Direct', a single Pi 0.85.1 agent loop on the same model (GLM-5.1), on 12 FrontierMath problems (3 runs each) and 40 Cybench CTF tasks (1 run each) under a 5-hour cap, with unsolved runs scored as 300 minutes. CAIRN halves mean FrontierMath solving time (53.19 -> 27.45 min) at 4.8x the tokens, but Direct is faster on 30 of 40 Cybench tasks at a quarter of the tokens. Stratified by Direct's token use, CAIRN is faster on 13 of 17 high-effort (>=1M token) tasks (47.20 -> 25.35 min) at 3.69x tokens, rising to 8.66x and 14.71x on medium- and low-effort tasks. Success rates are never reported separately from time. Code and prompts are public.

claims.claim: On high-effort tasks (>=1M tokens), CAIRN is faster in 76.5% of cases, with speedups up to 3.08x
claims.evidence: 13 of 17 tasks in Table 2's top stratum; mean time 47.20 -> 25.35 min at a 3.69x token ratio. Strata are defined post hoc by the baseline's own token use, which correlates with Direct struggling or timing out (unsolved = 300 min), so some of the effect may be regression to the mean. Cybench tasks are single runs; FrontierMath has 3 runs per problem.

claims.claim: As task effort increases, time gains grow while relative token overhead declines
claims.evidence: Token ratio 14.71x (low), 8.66x (mid), 3.69x (high); pooled log-log fit with task-bootstrap 95% band gives a break-even at 1.24M baseline tokens (Fig. 7). Overall CAIRN uses 5.58M vs 1.28M tokens and is faster on only 18 of 52 tasks.

claims.claim: CAIRN is evaluated on task success, time to solution and token consumption
claims.evidence: Task success is never reported on its own; it is folded into solving time by assigning 300 minutes to unsolved runs, so faster time and higher solve rate cannot be separated.

claims.claim: DAG coordination incurs higher token cost with no observable gains on low-effort tasks
claims.evidence: The paper's own negative result: Cybench Direct faster on 30/40 at 0.83M vs 3.22M mean tokens (Table 1).

claims.claim: More parallel worker slots speed up hard problems
claims.evidence: fm-02 with 1, 3 and 6 slots: 97.22, 73.70, 26.51 min, one run each (§4.3, Fig. 8).

claims.claim: The paradigm has strong external traction (about 3,000 GitHub stars; the only system to solve all tasks in a Tencent Cloud penetration hackathon; leading TSecBench result)
claims.evidence: Asserted in the introduction with no data; the hackathon and TSecBench are run by the authors' affiliated Tencent lab.

patterns.note: LLM-generated, incrementally grown fact-intent DAG with parallel workers vs a same-model single-loop agent (Direct) under the same 5-hour cap. CAIRN wins time on FrontierMath and high-effort tasks (13/17) but loses on most Cybench tasks (Direct faster 30/40) and costs 3.7-14.7x the tokens. The comparison is not budget-matched: no arm runs several independent Direct agents in parallel with the same token budget, so graph coordination is not separated from parallel compute. Prompts also differ between arms.
Reasoner plus up to 6 workers vs one agent, same model: faster only on high-effort tasks, at several times the tokens; no matched parallel-sampling baseline.
The single Pi loop is faster and far cheaper on low-effort tasks (Cybench 30/40) and loses on long, hard ones; break-even at about 1.24M baseline tokens.
Token use reported throughout (Tables 1-2); no budget-control mechanism is proposed or tested.
The persistent graph makes trajectories inspectable and auditable (§2.3, §4.4); no user study of whether it aids debugging or intervention.
Verified facts persist in the graph and are reused across workers; reuse is not measured separately.

methodology.sample: 12 FrontierMath problems (3 runs each) and 40 Cybench CTF tasks (1 run each)
methodology.baselines: Direct: single Pi 0.85.1 agent loop on the same model and time cap; no parallel independent-agents baseline
methodology.variance: 3 runs per FrontierMath problem, single runs on Cybench; bootstrap band on the effort-speedup fit only
methodology.ablations: Worker slots 1/3/6 on one problem, one run each
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; FrontierMath is held-out by design, Cybench is public
methodology.languages: Mathematics and CTF security tasks (shell, Python tooling)

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/oritera/Cairn; full prompts in App. B; reproducibility statement

biases.detail: Cybench tasks run once; per-task speedups have no CIs.
Solving time with unsolved = 300 min merges success and speed; success rates are not reported.
The headline 76.5% is 13 of 17 tasks; the concurrency study is one problem with one run per setting.
Strata are defined by the baseline's own token use on the same runs, which selects tasks where Direct did badly.
No same-budget parallel Direct agents (best-of-k or first-to-finish), so coordination gains are not separated from extra compute.
Stars, hackathon and leaderboard claims are unsupported and tied to the authors' own lab.

coi.affiliations: Nankai University; Tencent Security Yunding Lab; Tsinghua University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: The authors' own open-source CAIRN; GLM-5.1 backbone; Pi harness as baseline
coi.detail: Industry co-authors promote external wins at a hackathon and leaderboard run by their own lab, but the paper's measured comparison is open-source and reports CAIRN's losses.

verdict_reason: A same-model comparison with open code and prompts that honestly reports where the DAG loses (low-effort tasks, token cost). The caveats: one model, single-run Cybench, success folded into time, post-hoc stratification on the baseline's own outcome, and no compute-matched parallel baseline. These limit the high-effort speedup to a hypothesis about time-to-solution, not proof that graph coordination beats parallel compute.
applicability: For the Java team, an LLM-grown task DAG with parallel workers buys wall-clock time only on long, hard explorations (roughly >1M tokens for a single agent), at about 4x the tokens there and up to 15x on routine tasks. Typical ingestion-pipeline changes, bug fixes and spec-driven feature work across the 4+ repos fall in the regime where a single agent loop is faster and cheaper. A DAG coordinator is worth considering only for open-ended investigations, such as cross-repo incident forensics or security audits, and should first be compared with simply running several independent agents in parallel.

conflicts_with.detail: OpenCollab finds model-directed teams realize their declared organization in only 47.2% of runs and attributes gains to a code-scripted two-coder workflow resembling parallel sampling plus selection; CAIRN credits an LLM reasoner's graph dispatch but has no parallel-sampling arm to rule that explanation out.

E3-Orch reports RL-trained DAG orchestration with parallel subtasks at 1.16-1.59x better performance per token, whereas CAIRN's prompted DAG costs 3.7-14.7x the tokens of a single loop; training the orchestrator may be what makes DAG dispatch token-efficient.

Same batch: DAGent's incrementally grown DAG used fewer tokens than its plan-then-patch variant and outperformed linear loops on deep research. CAIRN, also incremental, is far costlier than its linear baseline, so incremental growth alone does not guarantee efficiency.
